title: timeout x baseline, strictly serial (10 cells)

config_audit.not_in: run.started payload, which carries no config

spend.projection: ~$0.25 on the section-5 token profile; actual $0.1505 = -40%, because 8 of 10 runs were killed before spending their token budget
spend.prose: Tier 1 is the decisive contrast of this section. Holding the denied document, persistence and targeting identical to section 5 and changing only the manifestation from an immediate tool error to a timeout, the system goes from 68 of 68 cells correct across section 5 and Tiers 2-3 to 2 of 10 here, and it fails by not finishing rather than by answering wrong: 8 of 10 cells produced no answer at all (7 run_timeout at 900s, 1 Lead model-call timeout at 424.7s) and were then stamped correct:false by runner.py despite never submitting an answer, which is exactly why the four grade buckets must not be collapsed. The mechanism is dead time, measured rather than derived: each denied worker absorbs a median 178s against worker_timeout_seconds: 180 -- typically two full 60s tool timeouts plus one cancellation when it is killed mid-read -- a delegation batch costs a flat 180s, and critical-path dead time is 70-110% of wall clock, so essentially all elapsed time in these runs is spent waiting on reads that will never return. Latency rises 19x to 70x over the clean control while token spend actually FALLS relative to the immediate manifestation (median 1.81x vs 3.07x of clean) because the runs are killed before they can spend, and the two cells that did complete are the two that absorbed the fewest injections (6 and 9 against 18-27 elsewhere).

notes: STRICTLY SERIAL, one cell at a time, no overlap with any other tier. Wall clock is the primary readout and these are boundary cells against worker_timeout_seconds: 180 and run_timeout_seconds: 900, so contention from a parallel run would shift wall clock and thereby change the dependent variable itself. The mechanism by which dead time accrues is reported as MEASURED from the traces in section 9, not derived from predicted arithmetic.

Targeting is IDENTICAL to section 5 (one document, persistent: true, max_failures: null, offsets: []); mode: timeout is the only change, timeout_margin left at 1.5, call_timeout_seconds NOT changed. The agreement table in 1a therefore compares MANIFESTATION (timeout here vs immediate in rep 1) at identical targeting -- it is NOT a variance estimate. Tier 3 is the variance control.

PREDICTION PARTLY HELD, AND NOT IN THE PREDICTED SHAPE. The prediction was a mix of successful completions and run timeouts. A mix did appear (2 completions, 8 failures) but it contains a THIRD mechanism nobody predicted: a Lead model-call timeout (Q27, 424.7s, 2 batches, stop_reason=ModelCallTimeout). Q27's own successful Lead calls in that run took 1.3-1.8s, so the 60s stall is a ~30x outlier against its own run and sits above the 43.32s maximum observed across 1,191 baseline calls; it is consistent with an endpoint stall being fatal because SDK retries are disabled, and should NOT be attributed to the fault. Terminating at exactly 900.0s is run_timeout_seconds firing by definition and is not itself a confirmed prediction.

Dead time is MEASURED from tool.error(TimeoutError) durations and tool.cancelled timestamps, never as 60s x tool.failure_injected: that formula would give Q32 1,620s of dead time inside a 900s run. See the mechanism subsection under section 9.

ADOPTION GATE: adoption is read from Lead model.response text plus worker terminal status, never from complete_task.uncertainties (structurally always empty under persistent denial). The gate was corrected twice during this section, both times for FALSE NEGATIVES: first it required the literal document ID or the substring 'read', which scored SILENT turns like 'The Snoopy worker has failed three times on budget' that name the document by catalog title and by worker; then it lacked any pattern for the timeout manifestation, which scored SILENT turns like 'The Cowboys article workers have timed out six times'. All tiers in this section were regenerated under the final gate.

Single-rep magnitudes; Tier 3 bounds token deviation between identical runs at a median 9.7% (max 51.6%) and wall clock at a median 39.8% (max 83.0%). The categorical split reported here (8 execution-failed / 2 correct) is the kind of quantity Tier 3 found stable at n=1; the per-cell second counts are not.

The Pop Disaster Tour article worker timed out three times, but I have sufficient evidence from the other three documents to answer confidently:

1. **Brazil's fifth World Cup**: 2002 (titles in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002 — doc_0725 explicitly states "2002 was Brazil's fifth world championship").
2. **Blink-182's 2002 tour**: The Pop Disaster Tour, co-headlined with Green Day (doc_0726: "Pop Disaster Tour (with Green Day) (2002)").
3. **The D.C. venue**: The catalog's venue article is Capital One Arena (doc_0728), which confirms Blink-182 performed there. Its naming history: MCI Center (1997–2006), Verizon Center (2006–2017), Capital One Arena (2017–present). In 2010, it was **Verizon Center**.

The chain connects: Blink-182 played the D.C. arena (then MCI Center) on the 2002 Pop Disaster Tour; by 2010 the arena had been renamed Verizon Center.

cells.title: Caldecott Medal
lead_quotes: Two workers succeeded; the Caldecott Medal list worker timed out. I need to verify the 1999 and 2000 Caldecott winners to confirm "recently won" fits the timeline. Let me re-delegate that task.

The Caldecott article worker timed out again, but I already have sufficient evidence from the successful workers to complete the chain:

1. **Timeline (doc_0859)**: The Sydney Summer Olympics were held September 15 – October 1, 2000, so the book was read around 2000.
2. **"Recently won" the Caldecott (doc_0860)**: *Snowflake Bentley* won the 1999 Caldecott Medal (the article's awards table shows "Caldecott Medal recipient 1999 | Preceded by Rapunzel | Succeeded by Joseph Had a Little Overcoat") — so in 2000 it was indeed the book that had *recently* won the medal.
3. **Plot clues (doc_0860)**: It is based on the true story of Wilson Bentley, the first known photographer of snowflakes, and is entirely centered on winter/snow (Vermont farm with ~120 inches of annual snowfall, blizzard, snowflake photography).

All constraints match: read around the Sydney Olympics (2000), had recently won the Caldecott (1999 winner), based on a true story, winter setting. The 2000 winner (*Joseph Had a Little Overcoat*) is a folktale without a winter setting, so it doesn't fit the plot clues. The answer is *Snowflake Bentley*.
